edge_858.relationship: Foucauldian analysis contributes to the concept of moral regulation and its governmentality reformulation
edge_858.evidence_note: Ruonavaara's abstract describes Corrigan and Sayer's framework as fusing Durkheimian and Foucauldian analysis with basic Marxist theory; Dean's abstract argues that problems in Corrigan's account are better formulated through Foucault's problematic of governmentality. PhD context: 46 of 107 PhDs citing Valverde 1991 also cite Foucault (43% vs 20% of all PhDs). Drawn as a contribution, the atlas's usual kind for Foucault's outgoing edges; an influence edge would need Valverde's own acknowledgement of the debt, which was sought (2026-10-12) but not found in checked text. Not a claim about every Canadian study in the roster.

edge_861.relationship: Protestant reformers as regulators and as religious actors
edge_861.evidence_note: Valverde studies the moral fervour of Protestant social reformers (publisher description); the religion-and-reform entry studies the same churches and social gospel as religious history (Christie and Gauvreau 1996, title-level). The two fields read the reformers differently; no critique is asserted because the checked texts do not state one. PhD context: 67 of 164 2009–2026 PhDs engaging Moral regulation also engage Religion, social reform & secularization in Canada (41%; lift 3.97), counted after removing shared anchors. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs. Valverde places moral reform at the centre of English Canada's race, class and gender order; Cook's Regenerators covers the same reformers' religious thought. PhD context: 25 of 42 PhDs citing The Regenerators also cite Valverde (lift 7.2). Comparison only.

cdn_national_tradition.label: Laurentian & national tradition
cdn_national_tradition.date_label: Staple studies 1923–40 · Creighton 1937 · Lower 1946 · Careless 1954 · Centenary Series volumes 1964–85 · Berger's analysis 1976
cdn_national_tradition.description: English-Canadian historical writing that took the transcontinental nation-state as its frame, from the interwar years to the centennial. Its economic core is the staple approach: Innis's studies of the fur trade (1930) and cod fisheries (1940) read Canada's development through exports to imperial centres, an approach Watkins later called Canada's most distinctive contribution to political economy. Creighton's Commercial Empire of the St. Lawrence (1937) simplified and expanded Innis's thesis, making Montreal's merchants the 'spiritual fathers' of Confederation; his Macdonald biography followed. Liberal nationalists such as Lower and Underhill and conservative nationalists such as Creighton and Stacey disagreed politically while sharing the nation-state as the frame of reference. Careless offered a metropolitan interpretation (1954), which Donald Davis (1985) found indeterminate, and Morton asked in 1946 on what critical premises the established interpretations rested. The Canadian Centenary Series, from 1964, gathered national syntheses, including translated volumes by the Quebec historians Trudel and Ouellet. Cook's and Careless's 'limited identities' (1967, 1969) and the new regional history of Acadiensis (1971) challenged the frame, and Berger's Writing of Canadian History (1976) analysed the English-Canadian tradition as a historiographical subject. French-Canadian historians such as Michel Brunet pursued a rival national vision, treated under Quebec historiography.

Macdonald (1952, 1955); Lower, Colony to Nation (1946); Underhill, In Search of Canadian Liberalism (1960); Careless, "Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History" (1954); Morton, "Clio in Canada" (1946) and The Kingdom of Canada (1963); Canadian Centenary Series volumes by Morton (1964), Neatby (1966), Trudel (1973), Brown and Cook (1974), Ouellet (1980). Restatement: Watkins (1963). Analysis: Berger, The Writing of Canadian History (1976, 1986); Buckner (2000); Miville (2016). Critics: Cook (1967), Careless (1969), Buckner (1971), Davis (1985).
cdn_national_tradition.scope_note: A teaching umbrella, not one school. The staple approach (political economy), Creighton's Laurentian narrative, liberal and conservative nationalisms, metropolitanism and the Centenary Series are distinct projects; roster inclusion is not membership. The label avoids 'Laurentian school': no checked source uses that phrase. French-Canadian and Quebec national historiography belongs to Quebec historiography: Trudel and Ouellet are named only in the Centenary Series strand, and the Creighton–Brunet comparison is carried by the relationship note, not the roster. Stacey (official history, external policy) is placed in Canadian military history and Political, international & national history; Stanley appears as a secondary row for The Birth of Western Canada. Critics appear as critics.

cdn_intellectual_cultural.label: English-Canadian intellectual & cultural history
cdn_intellectual_cultural.date_label: Berger 1970, 1976 · McKillop 1979 · Owram 1980, 1986 · cultural turn: McKay 1994, Vance 1997, Nelles 1999 · selected later readings
cdn_intellectual_cultural.description: English-Canadian intellectual and cultural history studies how Canadians thought about empire, nation, religion, science and the state, and later how traditions, myths and public memories were made. Carl Berger's The Sense of Power (1970) examined imperialist ideas of Canadian character and mission and argued that Canadian imperialism was one form of Canadian nationalism; his The Writing of Canadian History (1976) made English-Canadian historical writing itself a subject. A. B. McKillop, Marlene Shore and Doug Owram followed ideas into the university, social science, western expansion and the interwar 'service state'. Ramsay Cook's The Regenerators (1985) joined the field to religious history. Critics charged it with what Clarence Karr (1989) called a 'narrow, elitist, biographical methodology': group biographies of academics, journalists and clergy that said little about what most Canadians thought. Susan Mann Trofimenkoff (1979) had argued that a field anchored to nationalism left women almost invisible. From the 1990s a cultural history of invention and memory developed alongside it. Ian McKay's The Quest of the Folk (1994) showed tourism promoters and cultural producers refashioning Nova Scotians as a simple folk. Daniel Francis wrote on the 'imaginary Indian' and national myths, and Jonathan Vance on the memory of the First World War. H. V. Nelles, Keith Walden, E. A. Heaman and Ian Radforth studied pageants, exhibitions and royal tours, and Colin Coates and Cecilia Morgan the commemoration of heroines. Yvan Lamonde's social history of ideas in Quebec runs on a separate francophone track.
cdn_intellectual_cultural.representative_figures_and_works: Berger, The Sense of Power (1970), The Writing of Canadian History (1976; 1986), Science, God, and Nature in Victorian Canada (1983); Cook, The Maple Leaf Forever (1971), The Regenerators (1985); McKillop, A Disciplined Intelligence (1979), Matters of Mind (1994); Owram, Promise of Eden (1980), The Government Generation (1986); Shore, The Science of Social Redemption (1987); Litt (1992); Vipond (1992); Francis, The Imaginary Indian (1992), National Dreams (1997); McKay, The Quest of the Folk (1994); Vance, Death So Noble (1997); Walden (1997); Heaman, The Inglorious Arts of Peace (1999); Nelles, The Art of Nation-Building (1999); Coates and Morgan, Heroines and History (2002); Radforth, Royal Spectacle (2004); Igartua (2006). Critiques: Trofimenkoff, “Nationalism, Feminism & Canadian Intellectual History” (1979); Karr, “What Happened to Canadian Intellectual History?” (1989). Comparisons: Lamonde, Histoire sociale des idées au Québec (2000); Lears, No Place of Grace (1981).
cdn_intellectual_cultural.scope_note: English-Canadian by design; Quebec's histoire sociale des idées is a comparison (Lamonde). Intellectual history (ideas, intellectuals, the university) and cultural history (spectacle, myth, memory) are distinct strands with different methods. The religious strand is shared with Religion, social reform & secularization in Canada, postwar identity with Canada’s 1960s. Editorial observation, not a sourced claim: Indigenous people appear in this field mostly as settler representations (Francis, Heaman), which is a limit to flag in teaching. PhD evidence (2009–2026): engagement with the field's anchor scholars is steady (ratio 1.02; 1.14 in a fixed panel of 14 universities), while its older works are cited less; the classics are ageing, not the field. Owram's 'Intellectual History in the Land of Limited Identities' (JCS 24:3, 1989; abstract checked, not cited as a source) is a practitioner's self-assessment that also notes the field's nationalist roots and the differing methods of francophone and anglophone writers; it is not treated as a critique.

cdn_religion_reform.label: Religion, social reform & secularization in Canada
cdn_religion_reform.date_label: Allen, The Social Passion 1971 · Cook, The Regenerators 1985 · secularization debate: Gauvreau 1991, Marshall 1992 and 1993–94, Christie and Gauvreau 1996 · selected later readings
cdn_religion_reform.description: Historical writing on Christianity as a force in Canadian reform, culture and everyday life, and on whether and when Canada secularized. Its central argument came in 1985–96. Ramsay Cook’s The Regenerators (1985) read late Victorian social criticism as the sacred becoming secular, and David Marshall’s Secularizing the Faith (1992) followed Protestant clergy through a crisis of belief to the 1920s as “an era of drift”. Their critics attacked this as the secularization thesis. Michael Gauvreau’s The Evangelical Century (1991) argued that the evangelical creed adapted to Darwinism and higher criticism; Marshall replied in 1993–94 that attempts to dismiss secularization were premature. In A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996) Nancy Christie and Gauvreau argued that the Protestant churches reached their greatest cultural influence before 1940 and placed secularization after the Second World War. Behind the debate stands Richard Allen’s The Social Passion (1971), which made the social gospel central to the history of reform, though recent doctoral work cites it far less. Social histories of Protestant culture, Methodism, gender and leisure (Westfall, Semple, Marks) moved the question from doctrine to lay practice. Catholic history developed alongside: Hamelin and Gagnon’s synthesis of Quebec Catholicism, Perin on Rome, McGowan on Irish Toronto. Gauvreau later carried the revision into Quebec, tracing the Quiet Revolution to Catholic Action (2005). Later work studies irreligion in settler British Columbia (Marks 2017), distinguishes political from social secularization (Van Die) and treats religion as a vehicle of the liberal order (Christie). Moral reform as regulation belongs to a neighbouring field.

Both sides appear as historians. Catholic and Protestant histories have different genealogies; Irish Catholic history (McGowan, Perin) stays here. The Catholic Action revision of the Quiet Revolution (Meunier and Warren, Bienvenue, Gauvreau 2005) has its main home in Quebec historiography. liberal_order_framework.label: Liberal order framework
liberal_order_framework.date_label: State-formation roots: Curtis 1988, Greer and Radforth 1992 · McKay’s prospectus Dec. 2000 · debate volume 2009 · selected later readings
liberal_order_framework.description: A proposal to write Canadian history as the history of a liberal project of rule. Ian McKay's prospectus in the Canadian Historical Review (2000) offered a way past the impasse between socio-cultural and national-political history: map 'Canada' as the project through which liberal order (in Fecteau's paraphrase, an individualism of liberty, equality and property) became common sense in northern North America from the 1840s. Commentators identify Gramsci's hegemony and Fernande Roy's study of francophone business liberalism as its sources and link it to earlier state-formation research: Bruce Curtis on schooling and the census, and Allan Greer and Ian Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992). Constant and Ducharme's Liberalism and Hegemony (2009) tested it on rights, municipalities, conservation, families, women and racialized people, and First Nations. This entry reads the framework as closer to a history of capitalism than to moral regulation: its subject is how property, the individual and market relations became the terms of rule. In his 2009 reply McKay held that liberal order and capitalism cannot be conflated, yet after the 1840s could not easily be separated. Earlier social histories of seigneurial Quebec (Greer 1985) and Montreal's wage-earning families (Bradbury 1993) are read alongside it. Critics answered: Bryan Palmer argued that the framework sidesteps capitalism's changing structures. Jerry Bannister proposed a loyalist order before 1840. Ruth Sandwell found a-liberal families, and Nancy Christie faulted its neglect of religion and of women. Later histories of land, enclosure and taxation (Weaver, Greer, Heaman) carry its questions further.
liberal_order_framework.representative_figures_and_works: Roots: Curtis, Building the Educational State (1988), True Government by Choice Men? (1992), The Politics of Population (2001); Greer and Radforth, eds., Colonial Leviathan (1992). Prospectus: McKay, “The Liberal Order Framework” (CHR, 2000), drawing on Roy, Progrès, harmonie, liberté (1988). Debate: Sandwell (2003); Constant and Ducharme, eds., Liberalism and Hegemony (2009), with Bannister, Heaman, Curtis, Sandwell, Perry, Brownlie and McKay’s reply; the Underhill Review round table (Ajzenstat, Christie, Fecteau, Pâquet) and Palmer (2009). Liberty: Ducharme (2010), McNairn (2000). Transition to capitalism (read alongside): Greer, Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985); Bradbury, Working Families (1993). Property and capitalism: Weaver (2003), Greer (2012, 2018), Heaman (2017). Left history: McKay (2005, 2008).
liberal_order_framework.scope_note: A programme and its debate rather than a school: roster inclusion is not adoption. Curtis, Greer and Radforth wrote its roots before it was named; Christie, Palmer, Sandwell, Fecteau and Ajzenstat appear as critics; Bannister proposes a loyalist order for 1750–1840 (chapter title), its relation to McKay not characterized. Kept separate from moral regulation by the user (2026-10-12) as "a different project closer to history of capitalism"; that reading is editorial and is stated as such in the description. The overlap with histories of capitalism is noted in the description; it is not drawn as a link, because the fields have not connected (user, 2026-10-12). Greer (1985) and Bradbury (1993) are read alongside the framework, not as its roots or applications.

moral_regulation.label: Moral regulation
moral_regulation.date_label: International roots (Corrigan 1981; Corrigan and Sayer 1985) · Kinsman 1987 · Valverde and Weir 1988 · Valverde 1991 · critiques 1994–97 · Strange and Loo 1997 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries
moral_regulation.description: Studies how morality, sexuality, health and conduct were made objects of governance by reformers, churches, professions, courts and the state, and how regulation shaped the selves of the regulated. The concept came into historical sociology through Philip Corrigan's work (1981) and Corrigan and Sayer's The Great Arch (1985), which treated English state formation as a cultural revolution; Ruonavaara describes their framework as fusing Durkheimian and Foucauldian analysis with Marxist theory. In Canada, Mariana Valverde and Lorna Weir offered preliminary remarks on moral regulation in Resources for Feminist Research (1988), and Valverde's The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991) argued that Protestant social-purity reformers were not simply repressive and that they linked sexual health to racial purity and slum clearance. Kinsman's The Regulation of Desire (1987), and later The Canadian War on Queers (2010, with Gentile), examined sexual regulation and the national-security campaign against gays and lesbians. Studies of contraception and eugenics (McLaren), women, girls and the law (Backhouse, Lévesque, Dubinsky, Strange, Sangster), welfare and single mothers (Little), and postwar normality (Adams, Gleason) widened the field. Adams tied moral regulation to state formation through venereal-disease policy, and Strange and Loo surveyed law and moral regulation from 1867 to 1939 (1997). Critics reformulated the concept: Dean (1994) recast Corrigan's account through Foucault's governmentality, and Ruonavaara (1997) rejected a monolithic, state-only project. The liberal order framework (McKay 2000) is a separate entry, closer to a history of capitalism.

Critiques and reformulations: Dean (1994); Hunt (1997, 1999); Ruonavaara (1997); Valverde, Diseases of the Will (1998). Later readings: Sangster, Regulating Girls and Women (2001); Kinsman and Gentile, The Canadian War on Queers (2010).

cdn_working_class.label: Canadian working-class history
cdn_working_class.date_label: Earlier institutional histories (Logan 1948) · Labour/Le Travailleur founded 1976 · Palmer 1979, Kealey 1980 · debate over culture 1981 · gender and family 1989–93 · selected later works
cdn_working_class.description: Canadian working-class history took shape in the 1970s as a new labour history of class, culture and community, set against an older institutional history of unions, labour politics and industrial relations (Logan 1948; Abella 1973; Bercuson 1974). The Canadian Committee on Labour History founded Labour/Le Travailleur in 1976. Palmer’s skilled workers in Hamilton (1979), Kealey’s Toronto workers (1980) and their history of the Knights of Labor (1982) were among its early monographs. In 1981 Kenneth McNaught framed the contrast as ‘E. P. Thompson vs Harold Logan’ and, by a later account, objected that social historians took a revolutionary goal as history’s purpose; Bercuson questioned working-class culture as an explanatory framework, and Kealey defended class analysis and culture. Social historians of poverty and the state widened the field: Copp’s Montreal working class (1974), Finkel on business and reform (1979), Struthers on unemployment (1983). Feminist historians remade it from within: Sangster on women on the left (1989), Parr’s gender of breadwinners (1990) and Bradbury’s working families (1993). Rouillard wrote the history of Quebec unionism in French (1989), and Heron’s Workers’ Revolt in Canada (1998) took the 1917–25 upheaval as a national subject. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) attacked the linguistic turn in social history. In 2000 Morton argued that the journal’s founding team had concealed a decade of stasis. Later work turned to deindustrialization (High 2003), the history of the left (McKay 2008) and Indigenous labour and the settler order.
cdn_working_class.representative_figures_and_works: Logan, Trade Unions in Canada (1948); Abella, Nationalism, Communism, and Canadian Labour (1973); Bercuson, Confrontation at Winnipeg (1974); Copp, The Anatomy of Poverty (1974); Labour/Le Travailleur (1976); Palmer, A Culture in Conflict (1979); Finkel, Business and Social Reform in the Thirties (1979); Kealey, Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism (1980); McNaught, Bercuson and Kealey (1981); Kealey and Palmer, Dreaming of What Might Be (1982); Struthers, No Fault of Their Own (1983); Palmer, Working-Class Experience (1983; 1992); Heron, Working in Steel (1988); Rouillard, Histoire du syndicalisme au Québec (1989); Sangster, Dreams of Equality (1989); Palmer, Descent into Discourse (1990); Parr, The Gender of Breadwinners (1990); Lutz, “After the Fur Trade” (1992); Bradbury, Working Families (1993); Kealey, Workers and Canadian History (1995); Heron, The Workers’ Revolt in Canada (1998); Morton and Sangster in Labour/Le Travail 46 (2000). Later: High, Industrial Sunset (2003); McKay, Reasoning Otherwise (2008); Burrill (2019); Finkel on Palmer (2021).
cdn_working_class.scope_note: A national research field within labour history. The ‘old’ institutional history and the ‘new’ labour history are positions in a debate, not successive stages; Bercuson and McNaught are critics (their 1981 essays are now checked through Bercuson’s abstract and Finkel’s account of McNaught), and Morton’s 2000 critique comes from outside the new labour history. Marxist and Thompsonian resources are documented by McNaught’s title and Kealey’s defence of class analysis; no single theory is attributed to the field. Gender historians (Sangster, Parr, Bradbury) are treated mainly in Canadian women’s and gender history; they appear here for their working-class histories. Quebec labour history in French (Rouillard) is part of the field and of Quebec historiography. Poverty and welfare-state histories overlap with political history. Immigrant workers (Avery) are in the immigration entry; Indigenous labour is a strand, not a claim of adoption. Palmer’s Descent into Discourse (1990) is placed here as a critique of the linguistic turn, not as a critique of women’s history. McKay’s left history is a post-2000 contributor row; his main entry is Liberal order framework.

cdn_women_gender.label: Canadian women's & gender history
cdn_women_gender.date_label: Earlier women writers of history (recovered by Boutilier and Prentice 1997) and Cleverdon’s suffrage history 1950 · collections and studies 1976–79 · Collectif Clio 1982 · Prentice et al. 1988 · Parr 1990 · Left History exchange 1995–96 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries
cdn_women_gender.description: Canadian women's history studies women as historical actors in Canada and, increasingly from the 1990s, gender as a relation shaping work, family, politics, law and the state. Earlier women wrote national, local and regional history, recovered by Boutilier and Prentice (1997); Cleverdon studied the suffrage movement (1950); collections and studies of reform and women's organizations followed in the later 1970s (Cook and Mitchinson; Strong-Boag; Kealey). Two syntheses had different starting points. The Collectif Clio's L'histoire des femmes au Québec depuis quatre siècles (1982) rejected a male-centred history presented as everyone's history; Prentice and colleagues' Canadian Women: A History (1988) offered a collaborative survey. Studies of women and war (Pierson), women on the left (Sangster), working families in Montreal (Bradbury) and housewives in the Depression (Baillargeon) joined the field to labour and family history. Parr's comparison of two Ontario towns (1990) challenged assumptions about the separateness of gender and class roles. In the 1990s historians argued over whether gender history extended or displaced women's history: Pierson weighed the turn to deconstruction and Scott's theory of gender against experience and voice (1991), and Sangster's 'Beyond Dichotomies' (1995), by her later account, protested a hierarchy that set gender history above a 'limited' women's history; replies in Left History defended gender history (1996). Later work examined masculinity and gendered political languages (Morgan), sexuality and the law, and postwar domesticity and consumption (Parr, Korinek, Fahrni). Lévesque asked how far Quebec historiography had integrated women (1997); Quebec women's history is treated mainly under Quebec historiography.
cdn_women_gender.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier women writers of history: Machar, Skinner, Skelton, Esther Clark Wright, Neatby, Ormsby, Daveluy, as recovered in Boutilier and Prentice, eds., Creating Historical Memory (1997); Cleverdon, The Woman Suffrage Movement in Canada (1950). Debate: Pierson (1991); Parr (1995); Sangster (1995, 1996); Iacovetta and Kealey (1996); Dubinsky and Marks (1996); Lévesque (1997); Sangster's retrospect (2011). Morgan, Public Men and Virtuous Women (1996); McPherson, Morgan and Forestell, eds., Gendered Pasts (1999); Parr, Domestic Goods (1999); Korinek, Roughing It in the Suburbs (2000); Christie, Engendering the State (2000). Later readings: Fahrni (2005), Campbell (2009), Bienvenue on Daveluy (2018), Bienvenue and Dorais, eds., Profession historienne? (2023).
cdn_women_gender.scope_note: A Canadian research field joining women's history and gender history; the entry does not decide the 1990s argument between them. Quebec women's history (Collectif Clio, Lévesque, Baillargeon) has its primary treatment in Quebec historiography, where 91% of its citing PhDs sit; this entry keeps those authors' work on family, work and sexuality and a critique edge to Quebec historiography. Fur-trade women (Van Kirk) and gender and empire (Perry) are treated mainly in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history and Settler colonialism and appear here as comparison rows; sexuality, law and regulation overlap with Moral regulation; childhood and family with Childhood, youth & family in Canada. Palmer's Descent into Discourse is treated in Canadian working-class history, as a critique of the linguistic turn, not of women's history.

strands.title: Earlier women writers of history
strands.focus: Women wrote Canadian history long before women’s history was a field: popular, local and regional historians (Machar, Skinner, Esther Clark Wright), the independent scholar Isabel Skelton, and a few university historians, among them Hilda Neatby and Margaret Ormsby, the CHA’s first and second women presidents (1962–63; 1965–66). In French Canada, Marie-Claire Daveluy wrote on New France. Most wrote national, local, fur-trade or political history; only Skelton (who “sought to write women back into Canadian history”, per Coulter’s reading of Crowley) and Daveluy (Bienvenue 2018) are documented as writing women in. They are earlier women writers of history, not founders of women’s history. Boutilier and Prentice’s Creating Historical Memory (1997) recovered this work and asked how professionalization masculinized history; the editors note that their subjects come mainly from “the white, Anglo-Celtic segment of society”. Cleverdon’s suffrage history (1950) is the earlier study of women that PhDs still cite. Bienvenue and Dorais (2023) extend the recovery to French Canada (after 2000).

strands.title: Gender history and women's history: the dichotomies exchange
strands.focus: Whether gender history extends or displaces women’s history. Pierson’s 1991 essay opens on the turn to deconstruction and Scott. Sangster’s “Beyond Dichotomies” (1995), by her own later account, protested “the hierarchy being established between a superior gender history and a ‘limited’ women’s history”; replies by Dubinsky and Marks and by Iacovetta and Kealey defended gender history against her dichotomy, and she answered (1996). cdn_childhood_youth.label: Childhood, youth & family in Canada
cdn_childhood_youth.date_label: Sutherland 1976 · Parr, ed., 1982 · Rooke and Schnell 1983 · 1990s expansion (Comacchio 1993 to Gleason 1999; Marshall 1998) · selected publication milestones, not boundaries
cdn_childhood_youth.description: Studies children, adolescents and families in Canadian history, and the reformers, experts, courts, schools and welfare programmes that sought to shape them. Neil Sutherland's Children in English-Canadian Society (1976) traced the reformers who pursued social improvement through children. Parr's study of British child immigrants (1980) and her collection Childhood and Family in Canadian History (1982), Rooke and Schnell's history of child rescue and the welfare state (1983) and Bradbury's family economies of industrial Montreal (1993) tied the field to family and labour history. The 1990s brought studies of maternal and infant welfare (Comacchio 1993), the baby boom (Owram 1996), youth and the making of heterosexuality (Adams 1997) and psychology and the 'normal' family (Gleason 1999). Francophone work examined family allowances and compulsory schooling (Marshall 1998), juvenile reform schools (Ménard 2003) and the medicalization of motherhood (Baillargeon 2004). Comacchio treats adolescence as a sociohistorical construction (2006); Myers studies girls, the courts and the policing of children in Montreal and beyond (2006, 2019). John Bullen's review essay on recent approaches to child-welfare history (1985) is the one early critique found. Historians also ask how young people's own experience can be recovered: Sutherland on adult memories of childhood (1992), and Gleason's critique of 'agency traps' (2016). The field overlaps with women's and gender history and with moral regulation; residential schooling of Indigenous children is treated primarily in the Native–newcomer entry.

who_killed_debate.label: The 'Who Killed Canadian History?' debate
who_killed_debate.date_label: Roots: Cook 1967, Careless 1969 · Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' and the JCS replies 1991–92 · Strong-Boag's CHA address 1994 · Granatstein's book 1998 · CHR replies (McKillop, Palmer) and francophone reviews 1998–99 · CHR forum, Buckner, McKay and Osborne 2000 · Dummitt and Dawson 2009
who_killed_debate.description: A quarrel among English-Canadian historians in the 1990s over whether national history had been lost, taught here as a moment in the profession's view of itself, not as current practice: few recent theses cite its texts. It had two phases. In 1991–92 Bliss's 'Privatizing the Mind' argued that intense specialization had replaced older historians' concern with explaining the country, and asked historians to remember that their subject was Canada. A 'Point-Counterpoint' in the same journal answered him: Gregory Kealey's class history was 'neither privatizing, nor sundering' (1992), and Linda Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag asked whose 'national' history was being lamented. Strong-Boag's 1994 presidential address answered 'neo-conservative laments' by indicting an old history of white male elites. In 1998 Granatstein's Who Killed Canadian History? took the charge to a public audience. In the Canadian Historical Review McKillop (1999) argued that Granatstein's narrow national history was itself political legitimation, and Palmer offered a dissident view. Francophone reviewers answered too: Dubuc read a lament for political history; Dumont, an indictment of social historians built on wrong facts about Quebec schooling. It grew from the 'limited identities' of region, culture and class that Cook named (1967) and Careless popularized (1969). In 2000 Létourneau proposed a narrative of Canada beyond unitarist and fragmenting versions, Cook called identities contingent and multiple, Buckner revisited limited identities, and McKay offered the liberal order framework as a way past the impasse. Dummitt and Dawson (2009) sought to move beyond political-versus-social history.

Phase one: Bliss, "Privatizing the Mind" (1991–92), answered in the JCS Point-Counterpoint by G. Kealey (1992) and L. Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag (1992); Strong-Boag, "Contested Space" (1994). Phase two: Granatstein, Who Killed Canadian History? (1998), answered in the CHR by McKillop, "A View from the Trenches" (1999) and Palmer, "Of Silences and Trenches" (1999); Strong-Boag's review (1999); francophone reviews by Dionne (RHAF 1998), Bouvier, Fahmy-Eid, Jedwab and Slogar, and Dubuc (BHP 1999) and Dumont (CHA Bulletin 1999). Reassessments: Létourneau and the CHR forum (2000); Cook, "Identities Are Not Like Hats" (2000); Buckner, "'Limited Identities' Revisited" (2000); McKay, "The Liberal Order Framework" (2000); Osborne (2000). Later: Dummitt and Dawson, eds., Contesting Clio's Craft (2009); Hamilton (2012).
who_killed_debate.scope_note: A debate entry measured through its texts, not its people, and written as a teaching entry about the profession's self-understanding rather than current practice: any core debate text is cited by 34 of 1,303 strict 2009–2026 History PhDs (2.6%), falling to 2.0% in 2020–26. It has two phases: Bliss and the Journal of Canadian Studies replies (1991–92), and Granatstein and the Canadian Historical Review replies (1998–99); the 1992 JCS pieces answer Bliss, not Who Killed Canadian History?. Most participants' citations in the PhD corpus come from their other work. Bliss and Granatstein's scholarship is in Political, international & national history; Bliss's main entry is Political, international & national history; this entry keeps his debate row (user decision 2026-10-12). The replying fields are Canadian working-class history, Canadian women's & gender history and Canadian regional history. Several replies are characterized by title only (Gregory Kealey 1992; Kealey, Pierson, Sangster and Strong-Boag 1992; Palmer 1999). The exchange among the main protagonists was English-Canadian, but francophone historians answered Granatstein in RHAF, the Bulletin d'histoire politique and the CHA Bulletin (1998–99); no francophone reply to Bliss was found. Létourneau's 2000 CHR essay is the francophone voice in the 2000 reassessments. Quebec's own debate over national and political history (the BHP from 1992, Bélanger 1997, later the 2006–07 school programme) ran separately; its checked texts do not cite Bliss or Granatstein, and it is related here only by comparison. Osborne's school-history essay links to history education, which the atlas does not treat as an entry.

(1998), which named the debate, took the charge to a public audience (as McKillop summarizes it: academic historians had abandoned a national past for 'overspecialized and ideologically driven forms of history'). In the CHR McKillop (80:2, June 1999) argued that Granatstein miscasts the scholar as citizen and that his national history is itself political legitimation; Palmer (80:4, December 1999) offered 'a dissident view' (title level). Strong-Boag reviewed the book in Historical Studies in Education (1999; unread). Francophone historians answered the book too, as reviewers: Dionne in RHAF (1998); Bouvier, Fahmy-Eid, Jedwab and Slogar, and Dubuc in the BHP (1999), Dubuc reading it as a lament for political history as a discipline (first page); and Dumont in the CHA Bulletin (1999, read in full), who corrected its claims about Quebec schooling and called it a fierce indictment of social historians. No francophone reply to Bliss was found.

cdn_regional.label: Canadian regional history
cdn_regional.date_label: Morton's Manitoba 1957 · Ormsby's British Columbia 1958 · Craig's Upper Canada 1963 · 'limited identities' 1967–69 · Acadiensis 1971 · Acheson 1972 · Forbes 1979 · Friesen 1984 · Barman 1991 · reassessments 2000
cdn_regional.description: Histories of Canada's regions as places with their own economies, societies and identities rather than as peripheries of a central-Canadian story. Provincial syntheses such as Morton's Manitoba (1957) and Ormsby's British Columbia (1958) preceded the 'limited identities' argument: Cook (1967) suggested that Canadianism might be found in regional, ethnic and class identities, and Careless (1969) made the phrase a programme. Acadiensis was revived in 1971 (Windsor's initiative; Buckner editor), its first editorial faulting historians 'obsessed with the great "national" themes'. Acheson (1972) traced Maritime industrial growth under the National Policy and its subordination to Montreal capital, and Forbes studied the Maritime Rights movement (1979). Friesen (1984), Barman (1991), Conrad and Hiller (2001) and Waiser (2005) wrote regional syntheses, while Owram, Carter and Harris tied western and Pacific history to expansionist ideas, reserve policy and colonial geography. Ontario had provincial histories of its own (Craig 1963; Nelles 1974; McCalla 1993). Acadia became a growing Atlantic literature: Griffiths on Acadian history and identity (1992, 2005), Plank and Faragher on conquest and expulsion (2001, 2005), and Reid, Basque and colleagues on 1710 (2004). Francophone regional history worked at other scales: Painchaud on the Church and French Prairie settlement (a 1970s study, published posthumously in 1987), Landry and Lang's Histoire de l'Acadie (2001), and Quebec's intraprovincial regional histories, which Harvey contrasts with interprovincial regionalism. By 2000 McKay asked whether 'region' could hold the new histories of gender, ethnicity and community, and Buckner revisited limited identities.

Critique: McKay, "A Note on 'Region'" (2000).
cdn_regional.scope_note: A research field for Canada's regions (the Prairie West, British Columbia, the Atlantic provinces including Acadia, and Ontario) and the limited-identities argument. Provincial syntheses, regional economic history, rural history and regional identity are distinct strands. Indigenous and settler-colonial histories of the West and British Columbia overlap strongly (Carter, Harris) and are primarily placed in Indigenous–newcomer relations & fur-trade history, Settler colonialism and environment. Ontario has a strand of provincial syntheses and economic histories chosen by PhD citation counts; Acadia has its own Atlantic strand. The North and Newfoundland are small in the PhD corpus (about 18 and 9 titles) and get only this note. Quebec's regional history appears only as a contrast of scale. Roster inclusion does not imply that historians accepted "limited identities".

strands.title: Acadia (Atlantic)
strands.focus: Acadia before and after the expulsion of 1755. In the PhD corpus this is a substantial and rising literature: 101 of 1,303 PhDs (2009–2026) cite Acadian history works, 5.1% in 2009–14 and 8.9% in 2020–26, 23 of them at francophone universities. Griffiths, an authority on pre-1755 Acadia, wrote on its contexts to 1784 (1992) and the emergence of Acadian identity (2005); Plank (2001) and Faragher (2005) studied the British campaign against the peoples of Acadia and the expulsion; Reid, Basque and colleagues read the 1710 conquest from imperial, Acadian and Mi'kmaw perspectives (2004). Landry and Lang's Histoire de l'Acadie (2001) is a francophone university synthesis of Maritime Acadia over four centuries that sets out to recount the experience of the whole Acadian people, not only its elite. Most of these works are later readings, after 2000. Readers of this literature also engage Quebec historiography (lift 3.2): see the comparison with Quebec historiography.

strands.title: Ontario and Upper Canada
strands.focus: Provincial history of Ontario: Craig's Upper Canada volume in the Canadian Centenary Series (1963); Nelles on the provincial state and the development of forests, mines and hydro-electric power (1974); economic histories of the province (Drummond 1987, Ontario Historical Studies Series) and of Upper Canada (McCalla 1993); Baskerville's concise history (2005) as a later synthesis. Works were chosen by PhD citation counts (Nelles 34, McCalla 26, Craig 17, Drummond 15, Baskerville 12) and checked against catalogue and DOI records; no checked source frames Ontario within the limited-identities debate.
